title: Organizational Change and Culture
sequence: relevant from initiation (assess culture before choosing the approach and engagement) through closing (transition and adoption). Organizational changes can strike at any time; evaluate their impact as soon as they are known.

relevant from initiation (assess culture before choosing the approach and engagement) through closing (transition and adoption). Organizational changes can strike at any time; evaluate their impact as soon as they are known.

change management in the Glossary means moving people and organizations from a current to a future state (this topic). The change management plan of the Guide sets up the CCB and the change control system (Topic 29).

[Beyond PMBOK 8] = exam-relevant, but PMBOK 8 does not spell it out (ECO wording, common exam practice, mock-exam style). PMBOK 8 says little about handling organizational change in detail, so much of this topic is practice and is tagged.

toc.title: The Project as a Vehicle of Change
Evaluate the Impact of Organizational Change on the Project and Determine Required Actions (ECO)
Support the Organization Through the Change
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Organizational change A shift of an organization from its current state to a desired future state. PMBOK 8: projects, in pursuit of value, drive change in organizations, and programs drive significant organizational change
Change management (Glossary) A comprehensive, cyclic, structured approach for transitioning individuals, groups and organizations from a current state to a future state with intended business benefits. Not change control and not the Guide's "change management plan"
Current, transition and future state Before the project the organization is in its current state; the desired result is the future state; some projects create a transition state in which several steps are taken in a structured manner. Completing the project moves the organization to the future state and delivers value as the key stakeholders defined it
Organizational culture An enterprise environmental factor: vision, mission, values, beliefs, cultural norms, leadership styles, hierarchy and authority relationships, organizational styles, ethics and codes of conduct
Organizational structure How authority and work are arranged: fixed functional and hierarchical structures versus network-oriented ones; structure influences the choice of approach (Topic 03)
Team culture Each project team develops its own culture, deliberately through team norms or informally through members' behavior; it operates within the organization's culture
Team agreement Behavioral parameters and working norms the team sets at the start and upholds through individual and team commitments
Organizational cultural intelligence The enterprise's capability to perform effectively in culturally diverse, complex situations, recognizing differences without careless stereotyping
Transition and readiness requirements Temporary capabilities, such as data conversion and training, needed to move from the as-is state to the desired future state
Resistant stakeholder Aware of the project and its impacts but resistant to the changes; unsupportive of the work or the outcomes (Topic 13)
Change management specialist A role that supports people through change, alongside project managers, scrum masters, team leads and business analysts (Standard §2.4.3)
Readiness Beyond PMBOK 8 How prepared people and units are to adopt the change: awareness, capacity, skills and support
Adoption Beyond PMBOK 8 People actually working the new way; benefits start only here
Subculture Beyond PMBOK 8 The local culture of a department, site, region or partner organization inside the wider culture

2The Project as a Vehicle of Change

  • PMBOK 8 view: a project's purpose is to move the organization from one state to another to reach a specific objective. Success means the organization reaches the future state and gets the value key stakeholders defined.
  • Delivery is not value. Value appears when people use what was delivered. That is why PMBOK 8 asks for transition and readiness requirements (training, data conversion), a transition of the final product, service or result, and a plan to maintain value as the project closes and transitions to operations (Topics 10 and 35).
  • Two sides to manage: the product side (build, verify, accept, hand over) and the people side (readiness, engagement, training, support, reinforcement Beyond PMBOK 8).
  • Who does what: the sponsor gives visible backing, resources and barrier removal; the project manager builds change activities into the plan and engages stakeholders; change management specialists, the PMO and HR help where they exist; business owners and operations own adoption after handover; the team builds and supports.
  • Do not confuse the two kinds of "change": change control (CCB, baselines, change requests) governs changes to the project; change management moves the organization's people to the future state (Topic 29).

3Assess Organizational Culture (ECO)

3.1 What to assess

Dimension What PMBOK 8 says or implies
Structure Fixed functional, hierarchical structures lean to predictive approaches (preferred lines of authority); network-oriented structures suit adaptive or hybrid approaches
Management style A culture of managing and directing, with work planned and progress measured against baselines, fits predictive; a culture that embraces uncertainty, self-managed teams, flexible thinking and innovation fits adaptive
Risk and uncertainty Fluid schedules suit tolerant cultures; risk-averse cultures prefer detailed, fixed schedules (Topic 16)
Communication Flat organizations rely on open, informal channels; hierarchical ones use formal approaches. Culture is a key driver for tailoring stakeholder engagement and the communication strategy (Topics 13 and 20)
Decision-making Empowering versus specifying and checking; trusting local decisions versus asking for external decisions
Buy-in and trust Is there acceptance of the proposed approach? Trust that the team can deliver? Is the team empowered to own its working environment? (Section 3.4.3.3)
Capability and maturity Policies, ways of working, reporting structures and attitudes must fit the delivery method; established processes make delivery more predictable (§4.3.3)
Ethics and codes of conduct Part of culture as an EEF (Topic 06)
Attitude to change Beyond PMBOK 8 History of past changes, change fatigue, openness to failure and learning, informal networks of influence, incentives and rewards, subcultures (departments, regions, partners)

3.2 How to assess

  • Review the EEFs and OPAs: stated values, governance, policies, how earlier projects ran, lessons learned (Topic 31).
  • Interview and survey stakeholders; observe how decisions actually get made and how people communicate Beyond PMBOK 8.
  • Ask the sponsor, PMO and HR; note subcultures.
  • Use cultural intelligence: differences among regions and groups are real, but individuals are not stereotypes.
  • Revisit the assessment as the project and the organization evolve.

3.3 Use the result

  • Choose and tailor the approach: predictive, agile or hybrid (Topics 03 and 05).
  • Tailor governance: formal or light (Topic 12).
  • Tailor communication and engagement: channels, formality, level of detail, who to involve (Topics 13 and 20).
  • Set team norms: team agreements created at the start with the whole team, including newcomers (Topic 25).
  • Plan change activities: coaching, training, pace and support that fit the culture (section 5).

3.4 When the way of working and the culture do not match

  • Coach and tailor. An agile pilot in a hierarchical organization where managers expect detailed plans and signed weekly reports needs coaching for the managers and tailored reporting (for example milestones with iteration plans beneath), not a switch back to the old way and not ignoring their needs.
  • Use a hybrid where one part of the culture requires baselines and another benefits from iteration.
  • Pilot the new practice, show results, then widen it.
  • Do not force an approach on a culture that cannot support it, and do not abandon it at the first friction.
  • Teams from different organizations (contract, strategic partnership) need more up-front work to build a "one team" mindset: roles may be formal and less flexible, so clarify how everyone contributes.
  • Be open about biases (for example a belief that only a software-generated Gantt chart is a valid schedule); transparency builds openness and trust.

4Evaluate the Impact of Organizational Change on the Project and Determine Required Actions (ECO)

4.1 Typical triggers Beyond PMBOK 8

Merger or acquisition · restructuring or a new operating model · a new sponsor or senior leaders · a strategy or priority shift · budget or headcount changes · new policies, tools or approval paths · staff moving to permanent teams.

4.2 The steps

  1. Confirm the facts with the sponsor and governance: what is changing, when, and what is still unknown. Respect confidentiality; share what you may.
  2. Assess the impact across the areas in the table below.
  3. Determine the actions: continue as planned (and record the assessment), adapt within your authority, raise a change request where baselines move, escalate decisions on funding, scope or priorities, or recommend pausing or stopping through governance.
  4. Act and communicate: update the plans and registers, brief new people, agree transitions, tell stakeholders and the team what changes for them.
  5. Monitor and reassess: the situation may keep moving; revalidate the benefits.

4.3 Impact areas

Area Questions
Objectives and business case Do the objectives, success criteria and benefits still hold? Is the investment still justified?
Scope and requirements What changes in needs, priorities and backlog?
Schedule and budget New dates, funding, approvals? Cost of delay?
Resources and team Who is reassigned, lost or added? Capacity, skills, reporting lines, morale
Stakeholders and sponsor New decision-makers, interests and expectations; changed engagement levels
Governance and authority New approval paths, thresholds, policies and reporting
Contracts and vendors Terms, vendor consolidation, a different platform or tool
Risks and compliance New or changed risks; regulatory, policy or contractual obligations
Dependencies and interfaces Other projects, programs, systems and operations

4.4 Typical actions

If this changes Do this
A new sponsor or key stakeholder Brief them and reconfirm objectives, success criteria and support; update the stakeholder register and engagement plan
Team members are reassigned (for example to permanent product teams) Plan the transition with the new leaders; hand over knowledge; update the resource plan and schedule through change control
Strategy or priorities shift Revalidate the business case and benefits with the sponsor; recommend continue, adapt or stop through governance
Funding or headcount is cut Reprioritize scope or backlog with the sponsor; use change control; update the risk register
A new approval path or policy applies Update governance, procurement and compliance plans; inform those affected; adjust the schedule
A merger changes platforms, vendors or tools Evaluate the impact with the sponsor (integration, contracts, dependencies); re-plan; do not pause everything and do not carry on blindly

4.5 Decision logic

  • The value proposition is the primary factor in deciding whether to continue, replan, expand or contract, or end early (Table 2-2 governance scenarios; Topic 12). The project manager analyzes and recommends; governance and the sponsor decide where it is beyond the project manager's authority.
  • Baseline changes caused by organizational change go through change control (Topic 29).
  • Protect the team: keep work going on what is not affected, tell people what is known, and correct rumors with facts you are allowed to share (honesty and confidentiality; Topic 06).
  • Do not: pause all work or carry on unchanged · decide alone beyond your authority · spread unconfirmed rumors · reassign people or change scope outside the agreed process.

5Support the Organization Through the Change

PMBOK 8 expects the project team to support people through change (Standard §2.4.3) and to engage stakeholders so that support rises and resistance falls (Topic 13). Practice adds the following Beyond PMBOK 8unless noted.

5.1 Plan the people side into the project

  • Assess readiness: who is affected, how, how much, and how prepared they are.
  • Explain the why: the need, the benefit in terms each group values, what changes for them and what does not; use two-way channels.
  • Involve people in designing how the new way will work.
  • Plan specific change activities in the schedule and budget: communications, training, coaching, pilots, support channels, readiness checks. (PMBOK 8: transition and readiness requirements are requirements like any other.)
  • Make sponsorship visible: leaders explain and model the change.
  • Hand over adoption: the business owner and operations carry the new way of working after closure (Topic 35).

5.2 Manage resistance

Cause What helps
Fear of losing control, status or role (for example experts who fear losing discretion) Involve them in shaping how control, roles and decisions will work
No visible benefit; seen as a compliance burden or surveillance Connect the purpose to outcomes they value in their own work; share evidence; involve them in tuning the solution
Habit and preference for the old way (for example manual spreadsheet approvals) Plan change activities that address the preference: pilots, side-by-side use, simpler steps, support, measured adoption
Lack of knowledge or skill Targeted training, practice, coaching, job aids and help channels
Fear of the unknown or too little information Early, honest, two-way communication; a visible sponsor
Change fatigue or overload Sequence changes, show quick wins, check capacity
Distrust from past changes Listen, acknowledge, keep small commitments, be transparent
Misaligned incentives Align recognition and measures with the new behavior; work with managers and HR

Typical wrong answers: mandating use (breeds workarounds), training on features only (ignores the cultural barrier), arguing the strategic case (does not address fear of loss), escalating to force compliance (hardens resistance).

5.3 Reinforce and sustain

  • Celebrate quick wins; keep support available after go-live.
  • Measure adoption and benefits, not only delivery, and agree who tracks them after closure.
  • Fix barriers found after go-live (training gaps, workflow friction, incentives) with the business owner before declaring success.
  • Capture lessons and update OPAs (Topic 31).

5.4 Models you may meet Beyond PMBOK 8

Model Idea How it helps with scenarios
Lewin Unfreeze, change, refreeze Prepare people before the change; stabilize afterward
Kotter (8 steps) Create urgency; build a guiding coalition; form a vision; enlist volunteers; remove barriers; generate short-term wins; sustain the momentum; anchor the change in the culture Sponsorship, vision, quick wins, anchoring
ADKAR Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement (individual level) Match the action to the gap: awareness, communicate why; desire, involve and address concerns; knowledge, train; ability, practice and support; reinforcement, recognize and measure
Bridges (transitions) Endings, the neutral zone, new beginnings: the psychological transition people go through Acknowledge what people lose, support them through the in-between period, then mark the new start
Kübler-Ross change curve Typical emotional reactions: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance Expect different reactions at different times; listen first, then guide

The exam asks for the best action in the situation; spotting the gap matters more than naming the model.

6Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Culture fit Managing-and-directing culture, baselines, hierarchical structure Culture that embraces uncertainty and self-managed teams Mixed cultures; baselines where required, iteration elsewhere
Organizational change hits Formal impact assessment; change request and re-baseline through the CCB or sponsor Backlog reprioritized with the product owner; team changes revisit the team agreement Both
Engaging people Formal communication plan, training before go-live, readiness gates Frequent demos and early user involvement; feedback shapes the next increment Both
Adoption Larger cut-overs need readiness checks and support Incremental release allows phased adoption and learning Mixed
Typical risk Resistance discovered late Team reshuffles and constant change fatigue Neither side fully supported

7Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor the depth to the size and reach of the change, number of people affected, regulation, existing change management or PMO support, change history and fatigue, geography and cultural diversity.
  • Interactions: stakeholders (engagement, resistance), communications (culture, channels), governance (authority, thresholds, value proposition), resources (reassignment, skills), scope and backlog, risk, procurement (merger effects on vendors), benefits (adoption), closing (transition) and AI (adopting AI tools is itself an organizational change; Topic 08).
  • Check results [Beyond PMBOK 8 — practice]: stakeholder engagement moves toward supportive or leading; readiness gates are met; users actually use the new process; feedback is positive or improving; benefits appear after handover; team agreements are updated after membership changes.

8Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Organizational change (merger, restructuring, new leadership): evaluate the impact with the sponsor, then determine actions. Do not pause everything, do not continue unchanged, do not decide alone.
  2. A new sponsor must be briefed; reconfirm objectives and support.
  3. Staff moving to new teams: plan the transition with the new leaders; update resource plans through the agreed process.
  4. Assess culture before choosing the approach and the engagement style; culture is a key driver for tailoring.
  5. Culture mismatch: coach and tailor (for example reports for managers); pilot; hybrid. Do not force and do not abandon.
  6. Resistance: understand the cause and involve people; connect the purpose to outcomes they value. Mandates, feature-only training and pure persuasion fall short.
  7. Address the cultural barrier with planned change activities, not only with technical training.
  8. Value is realized by adoption: readiness and transition requirements are checked before handover; adoption is tracked after.
  9. Do not confuse change management (people and organization) with change control (CCB and baselines).
  10. Baseline changes caused by organizational change still go through change control.
  11. The value proposition decides whether the project continues, is replanned or stops; the project manager recommends with analysis.
  12. Use cultural intelligence; avoid stereotypes; adapt communication and team norms.
  13. Team agreements are co-created with the whole team, including newcomers.
  14. Keep confidential information confidential, but give the team the facts it may have and avoid rumors.
  15. Escalate impacts beyond your authority with analysis and options (Topic 30).

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Before planning engagement for a new regional office that will adopt agile practices, the project manager wants to assess its organizational culture. Which approach is best?

  • AUse the home office's culture assessment, since the company has a single culture
  • BReview documents, interview and observe people, noting subcultures
  • CAsk only the regional manager how decisions are made, since the manager knows best
  • DRely on national stereotypes about how people in that region work
Show the answer

Answer: B. Culture is assessed from EEFs and OPAs, interviews and surveys, observation of how decisions are really made, and input from the sponsor, PMO and HR, noting subcultures. Stereotypes, one informant or the home office's assumptions miss the local reality.

S2A project manager plans meetings for a regional team on the assumption that everyone from that country prefers indirect feedback, but several members clearly do not. What was the mistake?

  • ANot appointing a regional manager to speak for the team members
  • BChoosing meeting times that suit the project manager's own time zone
  • CStereotyping people instead of applying cultural intelligence to them
  • DFailing to translate the meeting materials into the region's language
Show the answer

Answer: C. Cultural intelligence means recognizing differences among regions and groups without careless stereotyping, so the plan is built on what the actual people prefer. The other options describe problems that the scenario does not mention.

S3A strategic partnership puts staff from two organizations with different cultures on one agile project, and the roles from the contracts are formal and rigid. What should the project manager do?

  • AImpose the project manager's home-organization culture on both groups quickly
  • BLet the cultures blend by themselves and review the outcome at closure
  • CInvest early in a one-team mindset and clarify how everyone contributes
  • DKeep the two groups separate and let each follow its own organization's culture
Show the answer

Answer: C. Teams from different organizations need more up-front work to build a one-team mindset, because roles may be formal and less flexible, so the project manager clarifies contributions early. Separation, imposition or hoping for blending leaves the cultural gap.

S4The organization cuts the product's budget by 20% midway, with no change to the release date. What should the project manager do?

  • AContinue with the full scope and ask the team to absorb the cut by working unpaid overtime
  • BReduce quality across all deliverables evenly, so that the schedule is unaffected
  • CPause all work until the organization confirms whether the cut is permanent
  • DReprioritize scope with the sponsor, use change control, and update the risk register
Show the answer

Answer: D. When funding is cut, the project manager works with the sponsor to reprioritize scope or the backlog, processes baseline changes through change control and updates the risk register. Cutting quality evenly, continuing unchanged or pausing everything ignores the impact assessment.

S5A new corporate policy adds ten days of vendor-approval time to every purchase, and the project has three purchases on its critical path. What should the project manager do?

  • AUpdate the procurement and schedule plans, inform those affected, and adjust the schedule
  • BContinue using the old approval path, since the project was approved before the policy
  • CAsk the vendors to deliver ten days earlier to absorb the new approval time
  • DSplit the three purchases into smaller orders to avoid the new policy
Show the answer

Answer: A. A new approval path or policy requires updating governance, procurement and compliance plans, informing those affected and adjusting the schedule, with baseline changes through change control. Ignoring the policy, shifting the delay to vendors or splitting purchases to evade it breaks the rules.

S6The plan for a hybrid team funds the build of a new system, but contains no time or money for training, communications or readiness checks. What should the project manager do?

  • ATreat transition and readiness as requirements in scope, schedule and budget
  • BRely on the vendor's user manual to prepare the staff for the new system
  • CAdd them only if the project finishes ahead of schedule and under budget
  • DLeave them for the operations department to arrange after the system goes live
Show the answer

Answer: A. Transition and readiness requirements, such as training and data conversion, are requirements like any other and belong in scope, schedule and budget, because value appears only when people use the system. Leaving them to others, a manual or spare capacity risks delivery without adoption.

S7Rumors of job cuts circulate during a reorganization, and staff on the project are becoming uncooperative. What should the project manager do?

  • ASay nothing about the reorganization until the sponsor makes an announcement
  • BTell the staff to ignore the rumors and concentrate on their tasks
  • CConfirm the rumors informally so that staff can prepare for the cuts
  • DShare confirmed facts, correct rumors and keep communication two-way
Show the answer

Answer: D. Fear of the unknown is met with early, honest, two-way communication, and the project manager corrects rumors with facts that may be shared while protecting confidentiality. Telling people to ignore them, confirming unverified information or staying silent feeds the fear.

S8Three other changes are landing on the same department this quarter, and its staff are exhausted. How should the project manager support the project's change?

  • APostpone the project's change indefinitely until the department feels refreshed
  • BSequence the changes where possible, show quick wins and check the department's capacity
  • CMandate the use of the new process to show that management is serious about it
  • DProceed on schedule, since change fatigue is a normal cost of any large change
Show the answer

Answer: B. Change fatigue is addressed by sequencing changes, showing quick wins and checking capacity so the department can absorb what is asked. Ignoring fatigue, mandating use or postponing indefinitely either overloads people or abandons the change.

S9Employees say they understand why the new process is needed and want it to succeed, but they cannot yet use the new tool. According to the ADKAR model, which gap should the project manager close?

  • AKnowledge and ability, through training, practice and support
  • BReinforcement, by recognizing and measuring adoption after go-live
  • CDesire, by involving the employees and addressing their concerns
  • DAwareness, by communicating again why the change is needed
Show the answer

Answer: A. ADKAR matches the action to the gap: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. Employees who understand and want the change but cannot use the tool lack knowledge and ability, closed by training, practice and support.

S10After the go-live of an agile release, the sponsor declares the change a success, yet users still struggle with workflows and training gaps remain. What should the project manager do?

  • AAdd the problems to the lessons log and leave the users to adapt over time
  • BWork with the business owner to fix the barriers and measure adoption before declaring success
  • CAgree with the sponsor and close the project, since delivery was completed on time
  • DBlame the users for resisting and ask management to mandate the new workflow
Show the answer

Answer: B. Adoption is when benefits start, so barriers found after go-live, such as training gaps and workflow friction, are fixed with the business owner and adoption is measured before success is declared. Closing, blaming users or relying on lessons alone leaves the value unrealized.

9.2 Recall Q&As

R1What does the Glossary mean by change management?

Show the answer

A structured approach for transitioning individuals, groups and organizations from a current state to a future state with intended business benefits.

R2How does change management differ from change control?

Show the answer

Change management moves people and the organization to the future state; change control (the CCB and the change management plan of the Guide) governs changes to the project's baselines and documents.

R3What is the project's role in organizational change, according to PMBOK 8?

Show the answer

Projects drive change in organizations: they move the organization from the current state, possibly through a transition state, to a future state that delivers value.

R4What does the ECO require under Support organizational change?

Show the answer

Assess organizational culture, evaluate the impact of organizational change on the project, and determine the required actions.

R5What does organizational culture include as an EEF?

Show the answer

Vision, mission, values, beliefs, cultural norms, leadership styles, hierarchy and authority relationships, organizational styles, ethics and codes of conduct.

R6Which cultures fit predictive and adaptive approaches?

Show the answer

A managing-and-directing culture with baselines and a hierarchical structure fits predictive; a culture that embraces uncertainty and self-managed teams, often network-oriented, fits adaptive.

R7How does culture affect stakeholder engagement?

Show the answer

It is a key driver for tailoring: flat organizations rely on open, informal communication; hierarchical ones use formal approaches.

R8What does PMBOK 8 check about culture when tailoring?

Show the answer

Buy-in, trust, empowerment and whether the organizational culture aligns with the project approach.

R9What are transition and readiness requirements?

Show the answer

Temporary capabilities, such as data conversion and training, needed to move from the current state to the desired future state.

R10What should the project manager do first when a merger or reorganization is announced?

Show the answer

Evaluate the impact on the project with the sponsor and determine the required actions.

R11What should the project manager do when the sponsor changes?

Show the answer

Brief the new sponsor and reconfirm objectives, success criteria and support.

R12How do you reduce resistance to change?

Show the answer

Understand the cause, involve people in shaping the change, connect the purpose to outcomes they value, communicate openly, train and support them, and plan change activities for the specific barrier, not only a mandate.

R13What is organizational cultural intelligence?

Show the answer

The capability to perform effectively in culturally diverse, complex situations while avoiding careless stereotyping.

R14Which disciplines does PMBOK 8 relate to the governance of project value and impact?

Show the answer

Change management, benefits realization, value management and revenue management.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
ECO task Support organizational change (Business Environment Task 7): assess culture; evaluate impact of organizational change; determine actions
Terminology Change management (organizational) is not change control (CCB, baselines)
Project and change Moves the organization from current state (via transition state) to future state; value comes with adoption
Culture as EEF Vision, mission, values, beliefs, norms, leadership styles, hierarchy, ethics, codes of conduct
Fit Hierarchical, managing-and-directing, risk-averse cultures lean predictive; flat, self-managed, uncertainty-tolerant cultures lean adaptive
Culture assessment Review EEFs and lessons, interview, survey, observe, ask sponsor, PMO and HR; note subcultures
Use of results Tailor approach, governance, communication, engagement, team norms and change activities
Mismatch Coach and tailor, pilot, hybrid; do not force or abandon
Org change hits project Confirm facts, assess impact, determine actions with the sponsor, act and communicate, monitor
New sponsor Brief and reconfirm objectives and support
Reassigned staff Plan the transition with the new leaders
Resistance Understand the cause; involve; connect to valued outcomes; plan change activities; not mandates alone
Readiness Transition and readiness requirements met before handover; adoption tracked after
Value decision Value proposition decides continue, replan or stop; PM recommends, governance decides
First-action pattern Evaluate impact with the sponsor, determine actions, involve and communicate, use change control for baselines
